sections.heading: THE BIG IDEA: HOW WE HEAR SHAPES HOW WE LIVE
sections.body: This message opens a three-part series on asking God for ears to hear, eyes to see, and feet to go and hands to serve. We begin with hearing because we cannot see the world as Jesus does or serve with His love until we understand the heart of the One we follow. The central question is this: have we become so familiar with the words of Jesus that we are missing the heart of Jesus? Our big idea is that how we hear the gospel shapes how we live it and share it with others. Sometimes it takes stepping outside the familiar to notice what we have stopped seeing in our own lives.

sections.heading: WHEN FOLLOWING JESUS BECOMES RELIGIOUS MAINTENANCE
sections.body: We live surrounded by Jesus: His name on T-shirts and billboards, Bibles on our phones, sermons and podcasts on demand. Yet familiarity can leave us hearing about Him more than listening to Him. Jesus' call to follow can shrink into a checklist: read, pray, attend, give, avoid the 'don'ts.' If we check enough boxes we feel secure, and if we don't we feel we have failed Him. Jesus never handed out a better list of rules. He called fishermen, ate with sinners, and confronted religious leaders who knew the Scriptures but missed the God those Scriptures reveal. His commands are real, but they were never meant to substitute for knowing Him.

sections.heading: ESCAPING THE MISERABLE MIDDLE
sections.body: Pastor Jonny Ardavanis calls it the 'miserable middle': we have learned what Christians should not do, but we have not learned to delight in the God who saved us. We no longer chase the pleasures of sin, yet we are not experiencing the fullness of knowing God either. Jesus did not come so that we could spend our lives miserable and trying not to do bad things. He came to give life to the full, life that begins when we know Him. This does not mean life is free of suffering or temptation. It means there is a joy that does not depend on circumstances, because David locates joy in God's presence, not in accomplishments or flawless performance.

sections.heading: ENJOYING THE EXPERIENCE OR ENJOYING THE PRESENCE?
sections.body: In Liberia, the church worshiped without modern lighting, sound, glass windows, air conditioning, or screens. What stood out was how much they enjoyed the One they had gathered to worship: they sang, prayed, and danced with real joy. We can be grateful for our facilities and still ask whether we have confused enjoying the experience of church with enjoying the presence of God. It is possible to enjoy the music without worshiping and to appreciate a sermon without surrendering to it. The better question after a service may be whether our hearts were turned toward Him, not whether church was everything we wanted.

sections.heading: WHOEVER HAS EARS, LET THEM HEAR
sections.body: Jesus said 'Whoever has ears, let them hear' to people who could plainly hear Him, because hearing and receiving are not the same. We can hear a call to repentance and receive only condemnation, when He is calling us out of what destroys us and into joy. We can hear 'love your enemies' and list reasons people don't deserve it, or hear 'forgive' and focus on our hurt rather than the mercy we have received. In the parable of the sower, the same seed falls on every soil, and the difference is how it is received. When we hear a sermon, we often think of someone else who needs it. We need to ask, 'Jesus, what are You wanting me to hear? What are You revealing about Yourself?'

sections.heading: FOCUS PASSAGE: JOHN 8:1-11
sections.body: At dawn Jesus is teaching in the temple courts when the teachers of the law and the Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery. They are not seeking forgiveness or answers. They are using her to trap Jesus. He bends down and writes on the ground, then says, 'Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.' One by one her accusers leave, until only Jesus and the woman remain. He tells her, 'Then neither do I condemn you. Go now and leave your life of sin.' Read the passage slowly this week, and let it be both a story about her and a mirror for you. The sermon draws three things to hear from it, covered in the next three sections.

sections.heading: HEAR THE STORY OF GOD'S LOVE
sections.body: The woman has become a means to an end: her humiliation is useful to the leaders. The Law held both the man and the woman accountable, yet only she is brought forward, and we should not invent details Scripture does not give. We do something similar when we reduce people to what we know about their sin and assume our opinion of them is God's. Knowing about someone's sin is not the same as knowing God's heart toward that person. In Matthew 9, Jesus tells Scripture scholars to 'go and learn' what mercy means, quoting Hosea 6:6, where the Hebrew word hesed speaks of steadfast, covenant love that does not vanish when we fail. Jesus came for the sick, not the already righteous, and He came because He loved us, not because we had made ourselves worthy. We can be just as harsh with ourselves, believing our failures put us beyond His mercy.

sections.heading: HEAR HOW GOD'S LOVE DEALS WITH OUR SIN
sections.body: Jesus does not say the woman is innocent or that adultery is acceptable. He confronts the accusers, turning the conversation from her sin to theirs. Jesus takes sin more seriously than we do and understands mercy more deeply than we do, and He never compromises holiness for love or love for holiness. Romans 2:1 warns that when we judge others, we condemn ourselves (the Greek word is katakrinō, which returns later in the story). The checklist mindset tempts us to compare ourselves with people whose failures are more visible and to feel less dependent on grace. But the publicly fallen, the privately struggling, and the fifty-year believer all live by grace, and no one graduates beyond it. The accusers 'heard' and walked away, but the text never says they repented. Conviction is not the destination, because it is meant to lead us to surrender.

sections.heading: HEAR GOD'S LOVE CALL US INTO NEW LIFE
sections.body: When Jesus says 'Neither do I condemn you,' He uses katakrinō, the same word as in Romans 2. The only One with the right to condemn her declines to. Some of us love the mercy and skip the call to change, while others cling to the command and barely notice the mercy before it, and both miss His heart. The order matters: mercy first, then 'Go now and leave your life of sin.' Repentance (metanoia, a change of mind and a turning) is not only about what we give up. It is about the life Jesus invites us into, and obedience becomes the joyful response of someone who has received mercy. In Ezekiel 36:26-27, God promises a new heart and His Spirit within us, so He does not just command a different life but transforms the heart it is lived from. A checklist cannot make us love Jesus, fear cannot produce joy, and guilt cannot give us a new heart.

sections.heading: DIFFERENT DOESN'T MEAN DEFICIENT: LESSONS FROM LIBERIA
sections.body: We tend to measure other people's worlds by what we are used to, and we can move from 'different' to 'better' without noticing. The same happens when we confuse our cultural expressions of Christianity with Christianity itself. The gospel is no more true because of where it is preached or the language it is spoken in. The Jesus worshiped in Liberia is the same Jesus we worship here, the same One who hears their prayers, loves them, and died for them. The Liberian church does not need to become the American church to be the church of Jesus Christ. Our comforts do not make us more faithful, and they may sometimes keep us from Him. All of us simply need to hear His voice, receive His Word, and follow where He leads.

sections.heading: WHERE ARE YOU STANDING IN THIS STORY?
sections.body: The sermon invites us to locate ourselves honestly in John 8. If you are in the miserable middle with a spiritual spreadsheet, Jesus is not standing over you with a clipboard but is calling you into life. If you have been holding the stones, quick to see what is wrong with others, let the stone drop, don't walk away from the conviction, and walk toward the One who has mercy. If you are the one standing exposed, hear Jesus say, 'Neither do I condemn you,' and let Him lead you into life to the full. Spend a few quiet minutes identifying where you are today and what you need to hear from Him.

sections.heading: PUTTING IT INTO PRACTICE THIS WEEK
sections.body: Pray the prayer of the series: 'God, give me ears to hear the story of Your love. Not just the parts that make me comfortable, not just the parts that affirm what I already believe, not just the parts that tell me what I need to do. Give me ears to hear Your heart.' When you open your Bible, ask 'Jesus, what are You wanting me to hear? What are You revealing about Yourself?' before asking 'What am I supposed to do?' Choose one familiar passage and read it as if for the first time. Then tell the story of a Savior who comes with mercy first and calls us into new life, to your family, your neighbors, and anyone you have been tempted to see only through their sin.

takeaways.body: 2. We can become so familiar with the words of Jesus that we miss His heart.

takeaways.heading: Jesus did not come to give us a better checklist but to invite us into a life we could never produce on our own.

sections.heading: SAME REALITY, FULLER PICTURE
sections.body: Pastor Bobby’s Liberian Grilled fish photo showed something real, but only part of it. When the whole picture appeared, nothing about the fish changed. Only the viewers' understanding changed. The same can be true of what we already know about God. We know Jesus died, rose again, and promised eternal life, but have we grasped what those truths mean? Pettiness, fear, anxiety, and constant complaining can shape the church just as they shape the culture. Last week's sermon asked God for ears to hear. This week we ask Him for eyes to see.

sections.heading: PAUL'S PRAYER FOR BELIEVERS WHO ALREADY BELIEVE
sections.body: Ephesus was full of competing religions and cultural pressure. Paul has already reminded the believers there that they are chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, and sealed with the Spirit. Then he says he has not stopped praying for them. These people already knew Jesus, yet there was more to discover. Knowing Jesus is not only a decision in our past. It is a relationship in which we keep growing. Paul prays for three things: eyes to see with wisdom and revelation, eyes to see our hope and inheritance, and eyes to see God's power at work.

sections.heading: EYES TO SEE WITH WISDOM AND REVELATION
sections.body: The Greek word for wisdom is sophia. The word for revelation is apokalypsis, an unveiling, like a curtain pulled back. Paul asks God to pull the curtain back for people who already believe. This is more than information. In Acts 19, new believers in Ephesus publicly burned sorcery scrolls worth fifty thousand drachmas, roughly fifty thousand days of a laborer's wages. They did not do it to earn God's love. They did it in response to a gospel that had already begun to change them. Revelation changes how we respond to God, and sometimes that means releasing what we are still holding on to.

sections.heading: THE CENTURION WHO SAW
sections.body: A Roman centurion guarding a crucifixion understood power, discipline, and what happened to those who challenged Rome. Crucifixion was Rome's public display of strength. The crowd demanded that Jesus prove who He was by coming down from the cross, but Jesus had come to give Himself, not to save Himself. After the darkness, the torn curtain, and the earthquake, the centurion exclaimed, "Surely he was the Son of God!" What the crowd read as weakness was God's redemptive purpose. We can witness what God is doing without fully understanding it, just as the Emmaus disciples later found that the facts had not changed but their understanding had. Wisdom is learning to see everything else in light of what God has revealed about Himself.

sections.heading: EYES TO SEE OUR HOPE
sections.body: Paul wants believers to know this hope, not merely wish for it. Everyday hope sounds like "I hope the weather is good," which expresses a wish with no certainty. Christian hope is a confident expectation grounded in God's promises and the resurrection of Jesus. Many of us find it easy to imagine everything that could go wrong, and years of disappointment can shrink our expectations until we stop imagining what God might do. Paul is not asking us to imagine things God has not promised. He is asking us to recognize the extraordinary things He has promised. Sometimes the greatest limit on our expectations is not what God has promised but what we have decided is no longer possible.

sections.heading: THE HOPE OF OUR CALLING
sections.body: The Greek word for called is kaleo, meaning to call or summon. God's calling is not just about finding a job or personal purpose. It is a gracious summons into a new life through Jesus. The New Testament says we are called into fellowship with Christ (1 Corinthians 1:9), freedom (Galatians 5:13), peace (Colossians 3:15), holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:7), His wonderful light (1 Peter 2:9), and eternal glory (1 Peter 5:10). Difficulty is real, but it does not write the final chapter of our story. Peter calls this a "living hope" because Jesus is alive, and it frees us from living as though everything depends on the next chapter.

sections.heading: GOD'S TREASURED POSSESSION
sections.body: Paul speaks of "the riches of his glorious inheritance in his holy people." Scholars discuss whether this means the inheritance God has prepared for us, or God's people as His inheritance. Scripture supports both. The God who owns everything, who needs nothing from us and is not made complete by us, calls His redeemed people His treasured possession (Deuteronomy 7:6; 1 Peter 2:9). Many of us measure our worth by accomplishments, possessions, appearance, influence, or other people's opinions. But our value is not something we must convince God of. His love was already shown in Christ, and our identity rests on the fact that we belong to Him.

sections.heading: SIMPLY WANTING TO BE NEAR
sections.body: In Liberia, children would come alongside the team and reach for a hand. They were not asking for anything. They just wanted to be close. Do we want to be near Jesus in the same way, not because we need Him to fix or provide something, but because being with Him is enough? Revelation 21:3-4 shows that the greatest part of our inheritance is not only that suffering ends and death is defeated. It is that God Himself will be with us. Salvation is not only what God gives us. It is that He brings us to Himself, and when we see the riches of what He has promised, we fear less what this world can take away.

sections.heading: EYES TO SEE GOD'S POWER AT WORK
sections.body: Paul could have pointed to creation, the Red Sea, or Jericho. He points to the resurrection instead. On Friday it looked as if Rome had won, but Sunday revealed what Friday could not. The same power that raised Jesus from the dead is at work for those who believe. This does not mean every difficulty disappears. It means our confidence is not in our own ability but in the God we belong to. Sometimes we focus so much on what we can see that we forget who God is.

sections.heading: OPEN HIS EYES, LORD
sections.body: In 2 Kings 6, Elisha's servant woke to find Dothan surrounded by an enemy army. The danger was real. Elisha, standing in the same place, responded differently. He did not ask God to remove the army. He prayed, "Open his eyes, LORD, so that he may see." The heavenly forces were already there, and the servant's circumstances did not change, only his understanding of them. His fear was based on something real, but not on everything that was real. Our limitations may be real, but they are not the measure of God's power.

sections.heading: NOT POWERLESS, BUT POWER-FILLED
sections.body: Some of us have spent years believing we are not enough because someone told us so, or because life knocked us down. This is not a promise that we can do anything we set our minds to. It is a promise that if we belong to Jesus, we are not powerless. The Spirit of the living God is at work in us, not because we earned it, but because we belong to Jesus (Ephesians 3:20). Paul says God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), so weakness is not a disqualification. We do not have to be powerhouses. We belong to the One who has all power.

sections.heading: CHRIST, THE HEAD OF HIS BODY, THE CHURCH
sections.body: Jesus is seated far above every ruler, authority, power, and name, and God appointed Him head over everything for the church. The church's future rests on His authority, not on our ability to impress. The church is His body, which means it is a people we belong to, not just a place we go on Sundays. Hebrews 10:24-25 calls us to spur one another on and keep meeting together. When someone is missing from the body, it matters, and we are called to reach out in love, not judgment. The body of Christ is also larger than any one congregation. The churches in Liberia have different buildings and resources but the same Jesus, gospel, and Spirit.

sections.heading: THE JOY SET BEFORE HIM
sections.body: The centurion saw the suffering of the cross, but we also know the empty tomb. Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross "for the joy set before him." Part of that joy is redeeming a people to call His own. You are His treasure, and He delights in you, rejoicing over you with singing (Zephaniah 3:17). Before we ever reached for Him, He acted to bring us near: Christ suffered "to bring you to God" (1 Peter 3:18). Seeing this should change how we face life, the future, God's calling, and the mission of the church, because Jesus is alive, reigning, and not finished.

sections.heading: THIS WEEK'S CHALLENGE: KEEP ASKING
sections.body: Paul wrote, "I keep asking." He did not pray once and move on. The challenge is to pray a prayer inspired by Ephesians 1 every day for the rest of the year, not as a formula but because every follower of Jesus should want God to answer it. Pray it in the morning and in the car, when fear shows up, when offense comes, and when you are tempted to believe you are not enough. The prayer asks for wisdom and revelation to know God more deeply, eyes opened to our hope and calling, an understanding of God's resurrection power at work in us, a life lived under Christ's authority, and faithful belonging to His church.

sections.heading: PRACTICAL APPLICATION EXERCISES
sections.body: Name one thing you know is true about Jesus (for example, He is risen, He is faithful, or He holds all authority) and write how it should change a fear or worry you face this week. Identify one "scroll" you may still be holding on to, such as a habit, belief, or source of security, and bring it to God in prayer. Write down one area where you have stopped expecting God to act, and ask Him to renew your hope there. Think of one person who has been absent from church, and send them a message this week saying you miss them and love them. Pray the Ephesians 1 prayer each day and record what you notice.

Do you simply want to be near Jesus the way the children in Liberia wanted to hold hands? What gets in the way of that desire?
Elisha's servant saw the army but not the protection of God. What are the armies you see right now, and what might God want you to see beyond them?
Where have you used weakness or inadequacy as a reason to disqualify yourself? How does 2 Corinthians 12:9 speak to that?
The sermon called us to remember people who may not be in church for a multitude of reasons... Who comes to mind, and what is one simple, loving way you could reach out this week?
